title: Add order lookup endpoint
bug: SQL injection: req.query.orderId interpolated straight into the query

posted.message: `orderId` is concatenated directly into the SQL string. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via `req.query.orderId`. Use a parameterized query/bind variables instead of string interpolation.

`req.query.orderId` is used without validating that it exists and has the expected type/format. If the parameter is missing or non-numeric, this will generate malformed SQL and likely return a server error. Consider rejecting invalid input before querying.

`orderId` comes directly from `req.query` and is interpolated into the SQL string, allowing SQL injection (for example, crafted values can alter the WHERE clause or append additional statements depending on the driver). Use a parameterized query/prepared statement and validate/coerce `orderId` to the expected type before querying, e.g. `db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?', [orderId])` or the placeholder syntax for this DB driver.

`orderId` comes directly from `req.query` and is interpolated into the SQL statement. This allows SQL injection (e.g., `orderId=1 OR 1=1`). Use parameterized queries/placeholders and validate/coerce `orderId` to the expected type before querying.

title: Add image conversion helper
bug: Command injection: req.query.path passed unescaped into exec

posted.message: `req.query.path` is concatenated directly into a shell command. An attacker can inject additional shell syntax via the query parameter and execute arbitrary commands on the server. Prefer `execFile`/`spawn` with argument array and validate or strictly whitelist the input path.

This helper ignores the result of `exec`, so conversion failures and process spawn errors are silently dropped. If callers expect the image to be produced, they have no way to detect or report failures. Consider returning a promise/callback and handling the error and stdout/stderr.

`req.query.path` is used without any validation or existence check. If the query parameter is missing or not a string, the command will receive `undefined` or an unexpected value. Was the intent to reject invalid input before invoking ImageMagick?

`req.query.path` is concatenated directly into a shell command passed to `exec`, allowing command injection (for example, a path containing `; ...`). Avoid invoking a shell for user-controlled values; use `execFile`/`spawn` with an argument array and validate/normalize the input path before passing it to ImageMagick.

All calls write to the same `/tmp/out.png`, so concurrent conversions can overwrite each other or return/read the wrong output. Use a per-request unique temporary filename/directory and clean it up after the conversion completes.

The result of `exec` is fire-and-forget: conversion errors are ignored and callers have no way to know when the output is ready. Consider returning a Promise and handling the callback/exit status so failures propagate and consumers only use the output after the process completes.

`req.query.path` is concatenated directly into a shell command passed to `exec`, which allows command injection (e.g., shell metacharacters in query input). Use `execFile`/`spawn` with argument arrays and strict validation/allowlisting of input paths instead of building a shell string.

`exec` is invoked without handling callback/promise results, so conversion failures and stderr are silently ignored. This makes failures hard to detect and can lead to inconsistent behavior. Capture and handle `error`, exit status, and output.

title: Serve uploaded avatar
bug: Path traversal: req.query.file (e.g. ../../etc/passwd) read with no sanitization

posted.message: `req.query.file` is concatenated directly into a filesystem path. An attacker can supply values like `../` sequences to read files outside `./uploads`, leading to arbitrary file disclosure. Resolve and validate the path against the uploads root before reading it, or restrict the value to a known filename format.

`readFileSync` will throw if the file does not exist or the query parameter is missing/undefined, which can turn a bad request into an uncaught exception unless the caller handles it. Consider validating `req.query.file` and returning a controlled error response instead of letting the exception propagate.

`req.query.file` is concatenated directly into a filesystem path, allowing path traversal such as `?file=../../etc/passwd` to read files outside `./uploads`. Validate against an allowlist of stored avatar filenames/IDs, normalize and ensure the resolved path stays within the uploads directory, and reject absolute paths or `..` segments.

`readFileSync` runs on the request path and will block the Node.js event loop for the duration of the disk read; a large or slow file can stall all concurrent requests. Prefer an async read/streaming response with file size limits and proper error handling.

`req.query.file` is concatenated directly into a filesystem path, which enables path traversal (e.g., `?file=../../etc/passwd`) and arbitrary file disclosure. Restrict to a safe filename format and resolve against a fixed base directory, then verify the resolved path stays within that directory before reading.

Using `readFileSync` in a request path blocks the Node.js event loop for the duration of disk I/O, which can significantly degrade throughput under concurrent traffic. Prefer async I/O (`fs.promises.readFile` or streaming) to avoid blocking.

`readFileSync` throws when the file is missing or unreadable, and there is no error handling here. A malformed or absent `req.query.file` will likely result in an unhandled exception/500 response. Add validation and catch filesystem errors to return controlled HTTP statuses (e.g., 400/404).

title: Sum cart totals
bug: Off-by-one: loop uses <= length, reads items[length] (out of bounds / undefined)

posted.message: The loop uses `i <= items.length`, so it iterates one step past the last element. On the final iteration `items[i]` is `undefined`, and `items[i].price` will throw. Change the condition to `i < items.length`.

`items[i].price` is used without validating that each item exists and has a numeric `price`. If a cart contains a missing entry or a malformed object, the total becomes `NaN` or throws. Consider guarding inputs or defaulting invalid prices to 0.
The loop condition uses `i <= items.length`, so the final iteration reads `items[items.length]`, which is `undefined`; `items[i].price` then throws. Use `i < items.length` or iterate with `for...of`.

The loop condition uses `i <= items.length`, which iterates one step too far. On the last iteration `items[i]` is `undefined`, so `items[i].price` throws a runtime error (`Cannot read properties of undefined`). Change the condition to `i < items.length`.

title: Gate admin panel
bug: Assignment in condition: if (user.role = 'admin') assigns, always truthy -> auth bypass

posted.message: This uses assignment (`=`) instead of comparison, so it always sets `user.role` to `'admin'` and returns true for any non-falsy user object. As written, the admin gate is effectively bypassed. Use a strict comparison like `user.role === 'admin'` instead.

This uses assignment (`user.role = 'admin'`) instead of comparison, so any truthy `user` will be granted admin access and have their role mutated to `admin`. Use a strict comparison such as `user?.role === 'admin'` to avoid both the bypass and null/undefined crashes.

`if (user.role = 'admin')` uses assignment instead of comparison, which sets `user.role` to `'admin'` and makes the condition truthy. This effectively grants admin access to any user and mutates the input object. Use a strict comparison (`===`) instead.

Revoke/rotate this key immediately, remove it from git history if needed, and load the key from a secure environment variable or secrets manager instead.

title: Generate password reset token
bug: Insecure randomness: Math.random() used to mint a security-sensitive reset token

posted.message: `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure, so password reset tokens generated here may be predictable. An attacker with enough observations can potentially guess valid tokens. Use a CSPRNG instead (for example `crypto.randomBytes`/`crypto.getRandomValues`) and encode the result.

Password reset tokens must be unpredictable, but `Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure and can be predictable depending on the runtime. This could allow an attacker to guess or reproduce reset tokens. Use a CSPRNG instead, e.g. Node's `crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('base64url')` or `crypto.randomUUID()` if the entropy/format is acceptable.

`Math.random()` is not cryptographically secure and should not be used for password reset tokens. An attacker can potentially predict tokens and hijack password-reset flows. Use a CSPRNG instead (e.g., `crypto.randomBytes(...)` / `crypto.randomUUID()` in Node/Web Crypto), and ensure sufficient entropy and fixed length.

title: Charge customer on checkout
bug: Empty catch swallows the payment error; checkout reports success even when the charge failed

posted.message: The result of `gateway.charge(...)` is ignored and `ok` is never updated, so `checkout()` always returns `{ success: true }` even when the payment fails or throws. Callers will treat failed charges as successful orders.

The catch block swallows every exception from the payment gateway. If charging fails, the function silently continues and still reports success, making failures impossible to detect or retry. Consider surfacing the error or returning a failure response.

`ok` is initialized to `true` and never changed, while the `catch` block swallows any `gateway.charge` exception. If the charge fails, `checkout` still returns `{ success: true }`, which can mark unpaid orders as successful. Set `ok = false` in the catch block, or let the error propagate and have callers handle the failed checkout.

`success` is always returned as `true` because `ok` is initialized to `true` and never updated in the `catch` block. If `gateway.charge(...)` throws, checkout still reports success, which can cause order/payment state corruption. Set `ok = false` in `catch` (or rethrow and let callers handle failure).

The `catch` block silently swallows all charge errors. This hides gateway failures from callers and observability tooling. Consider rethrowing, returning an error reason, or at least logging/recording the exception.
